extracted.intended_audience: fiction/creative writers working on dialogue and manuscript mechanics
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidelines for placing, punctuating, and choosing dialogue tags in fiction writing, including frequency, use of action beats, internal thought formatting, and genre conventions. Emphasizes clarity and industry standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make dialogue easy to understand and read
rubrics_metrics.description: Make your dialogue easy for your readers to understand and read.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the overriding principle: clarity and readability trump ornament. If tags, placement, or verb choice make dialogue choppy, incoherent, or distracting, simplify. 'Simple is always better.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Tag placement — Before the dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: When dialogue tags are before the dialogue, it looks like: Meghan asked, “Are you coming to my party?”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a comma after the tag. If the dialogue is the beginning of a sentence, capitalize the first letter. End the dialogue with the appropriate punctuation (period, exclamation point, or question mark), but keep it INSIDE the quotation marks. The guidance follows standard American English punctuation rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tag placement — After the dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: When dialogue tags are used after the lines of dialogue, it looks like: “Are you coming to my party?” Meghan asked. or “Are you coming to my party?” asked Meghan.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Punctuation still goes INSIDE quotation marks. Unless the tag begins with a proper noun, it is not capitalized. End the tag with appropriate punctuation. Avoid unnecessary capitalization of the tag.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tag placement — In the middle of the dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: When dialogue tags are used in the middle of dialogue, it looks like: “The car lights,” she explained, “aren't bright enough to drive at night.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A comma is used before the tag and goes INSIDE quotation marks. Unless the tag begins with a proper noun, it is not capitalized. A comma is used after the tag, OUTSIDE of quotation marks, to reintroduce the dialogue. End the dialogue with the appropriate punctuation (period, exclamation mark, or question mark) inside the quotation marks.

rubrics_metrics.name: How often to use dialogue tags (frequency and economy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use dialogue tags only as often as necessary to make speaker identity clear; fewer tags for short dialogue or when speakers are already clear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short lines of dialogue where each line is only a few words can use fewer tags. Excessive tags become unnecessary and distracting (tags almost as long as the dialogue). If characters are previously introduced or there are only two speakers, many tags can be removed to speed the reading. For conversations with multiple (three or more) characters, use only enough tags to clearly indicate who is speaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use action beats instead of tags
rubrics_metrics.description: You can use action or description as the dialogue tag (an action beat) rather than an explicit speech verb.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Jen looked down. “It's good to see you.” “Yeah, you too,” Ben said, biting the inside of his lip. Action beats can replace 'said' and provide stage business and pacing. Decide whether to include an explicit tag like 'Ben said' or let the action alone identify the speaker.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal dialogue formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: Industry standard is to eliminate the quotation marks and put the thoughts in italics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: I hope she doesn't ask me to drive, he thought. You may still use an attribution (he thought) if it makes the line clearer for readers. Use italics for thought and omit quotation marks to distinguish internal dialogue from spoken dialogue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of tag verbs — the 'said' debate
rubrics_metrics.description: There is debate over whether to use only 'said'/'asked' or to vary tags with more descriptive verbs (whispered, yelled, remarked, argued).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'Pro-Said' view: extra verbs are distracting; 'said' is easily ignored so readers focus on dialogue. The 'Said Haters' argue varied tags better convey tone. The recommendation: learn the industry standard for your genre, model published writers, and only deviate with a clear purpose and awareness that it may meet resistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punctuation rule for dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: End the dialogue with the appropriate punctuation (period, exclamation point, or question mark), but keep it INSIDE the quotation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rule is reiterated across tag-placement contexts: commas before tags go inside quotes; end punctuation for the spoken sentence remains inside quotation marks in American English.
